title: Lean In
author: Andrea Chiarelli
summary: Through a short fable written by a guest collaborator and a diagnosis by Chiarelli, this piece shows how a motivational phrase can stand in for a delivery plan. A team lead tells his team to lean in, nobody asks what that means, questions go unasked, one member works three late nights polishing, and the team later learns the deadline had already moved. The diagnosis is that ambiguity gets paid for in overwork, silence is mistaken for agreement, and a schedule change was treated as an FYI instead of a control signal. The author then lists a minimum structure: define the work before dividing it, share control signals early, add decision checkpoints, legitimise questions and set boundaries on overwork. It belongs in Leadership because it is about team coordination and what a leader owes a team under pressure.
points: A high-energy phrase such as lean in, used where a team needs priorities, decision rights and acceptable risk, is the early sign of a failing system.
Teams pay for ambiguity with extra hours because questions feel like delay and polishing becomes the socially acceptable form of escalation.
Withholding a deadline change until after the cost is paid is a leadership failure, since constraints are control signals that should change behaviour at once.
A fifteen-minute checkpoint at the end of day one, with explicit questions on scope, assumptions and risk, would have prevented the rework.
Assigning someone the role of person who slows things down makes questions quality control and lowers the social cost of asking.
quotes: In such an environment, the safest move is to produce more work, because more work can be defended. The cost is that the work stops being steered.

The team hears reassurance (“you’re capable”) but receives no operational definition of priorities, decision rights or acceptable risk. Nobody asks what “lean in” means because the social penalty is obvious: asking would signal doubt and force the lead to be specific.

By days two and three, the team is trapped in some sort of revision momentum: once you start paying for ambiguity with extra hours, it becomes harder to stop, because stopping would force you to discuss the ambiguity explicitly. The absence of objections is, once again, the predictable outcome of a context where objections are framed as delay.

If the deadline was even potentially flexible, the team needed to know that on day one, not after three nights of revisions. When timelines shift, plans should shift with them. Treating that as an “FYI” is irresponsible and, quite frankly, poor leadership.

The other shift is to protect questions as part of delivery rather than treating them as friction. In the story, the team avoided being “the person who slowed things down.” In a healthy team, the person who slows things down at the right moment is doing quality control.

Many teams burn out because ambiguity is allowed to sit in the middle of the room while everyone behaves as if it had been resolved. “Lean in” becomes a norm: do more, ask less, absorb the mess. For a while, that looks like commitment, but what really happens is that the team stops coordinating judgement through conversation and starts paying for uncertainty with extra hours.

The practical takeaway is to try and notice moments where a team is asked for effort without being given the conditions for good judgement. That is the moment to insist on definitions, priorities, and a short decision checkpoint, even if it slows things for a moment.
